Yet the picture becomes more complicated when yields are taken into account. Because organic crops typically produce around 20 to 25 percent less food per hectare, feeding the same number of people organically would require more farmland, which could mean clearing forests and other natural habitats. Some researchers therefore argue that the debate should not be framed as organic versus conventional. Instead, they suggest combining the best practices of both, such as using precise amounts of fertiliser, rotating crops and protecting hedgerows, while keeping yields high. The most sustainable farm, they conclude, may be one that refuses to fit neatly into either category.

Smallpox, a highly contagious disease that killed around 30 percent of those infected, is estimated to have caused some 300 million deaths in the twentieth century alone. In 1967 the World Health Organization launched an intensified campaign to eradicate it. Vaccinating everyone on the planet was impossible, so health workers adopted a strategy called 'ring vaccination': whenever a case was reported, they quickly identified and vaccinated the patient's contacts, and then the contacts of those contacts, creating a barrier of immunity around the outbreak. Offering rewards to people who reported cases also proved effective. The last naturally occurring case was recorded in Somalia in 1977, and in 1980 the disease was officially declared eradicated. It remains the only human disease ever to have been wiped out, an achievement made possible partly because smallpox infected only humans and produced visible symptoms, making cases easy to identify.

In 1901 sponge divers exploring a Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera recovered a lump of corroded bronze and wood that attracted little attention at first. Only later did researchers notice that it contained precisely cut gear wheels. Decades of study, including X-ray scans in the 2000s, have revealed that the Antikythera mechanism, built around 2,100 years ago, was an astonishingly sophisticated device. By turning a handle, its user could predict the positions of the Sun and Moon, the phases of the Moon and even eclipses years in advance. It also tracked the four-year cycle of athletic games, including the Olympics. Nothing of comparable complexity is known from the following thousand years, which has led some historians to describe it as the world's first analogue computer. Who built it, and whether other such devices existed, remain open questions.

Universal basic income (UBI) is the idea that every adult citizen should receive a regular, unconditional payment from the state, regardless of whether they work. Supporters from both the political left and right have championed it for different reasons: some see it as a way to eliminate poverty, while others value its simplicity compared with complex welfare systems full of rules and paperwork. Critics raise two main objections. First, a payment large enough to live on would be extremely expensive and might require substantial tax increases. Second, they fear that people would lose the incentive to work. Experiments have so far offered some reassurance on the second point. In a two-year trial in Finland, unemployed participants who received a monthly payment worked slightly more days than a comparison group, and they reported lower stress. However, such trials are small and temporary, so they cannot show how a permanent, nationwide scheme would affect the economy.

For centuries, the European eel was one of nature's great mysteries. Eels were common in rivers across Europe, yet nobody had ever seen them mate or found their eggs. Aristotle even suggested that they emerged spontaneously from mud. The puzzle was partly solved in the early twentieth century by the Danish scientist Johannes Schmidt, who spent nearly two decades collecting tiny eel larvae from the Atlantic. He noticed that the larvae became smaller the further west he sailed, and he concluded that the eels must breed in the Sargasso Sea, more than 5,000 kilometres from Europe. The larvae drift with ocean currents for up to three years before reaching European coasts and swimming up rivers. Remarkably, no one has yet observed adult eels spawning in the wild, and the species is now critically endangered, with numbers having fallen by more than 90 percent since the 1980s.

Every summer, a growing number of holiday resorts advertise 'digital detox' packages: guests hand over their phones at reception and spend a week without screens. The appeal is understandable. Surveys show that many adults check their phones dozens of times an hour and feel anxious when separated from them. Yet the concept deserves closer scrutiny. Research on the benefits of brief breaks from technology has produced mixed results; some studies report improved mood and sleep, while others find no lasting effect once people return to their normal routines. Critics also point out that framing technology as a poison to be purged encourages an all-or-nothing approach, whereas what most people need are sustainable daily habits, such as turning off non-essential notifications or keeping phones out of the bedroom. A week of abstinence, followed by fifty-one weeks of the same behaviour as before, may be little more than an expensive ritual.

Zero seems so obvious to us that it is easy to forget how long it took humanity to accept it. Ancient Babylonians used a placeholder symbol to show an empty position in numbers, much as we write 0 in 205, but they did not treat it as a number in its own right. The Greeks, despite their brilliance in geometry, were deeply uneasy with the idea of 'nothing' as a quantity. It was Indian mathematicians who took the decisive step. In a work written in 628 AD, Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero, such as that a number minus itself equals zero. The concept then travelled to the Islamic world and later to Europe, where it met resistance. In 1299 the city of Florence even banned the use of Hindu-Arabic numerals in official accounts, partly because a zero could easily be altered into a 6 or a 9 to commit fraud.

Beavers are often called 'ecosystem engineers' because few animals reshape their environment as dramatically. By felling trees and building dams from branches and mud, they turn streams into chains of ponds and wetlands. These new habitats support fish, amphibians, insects and birds, and they store water, which reduces flooding downstream during heavy rain and keeps rivers flowing during droughts. Beaver ponds also trap sediment and pollutants, improving water quality. Hunted for their fur, beavers disappeared from Britain around 400 years ago. In recent decades, however, they have been reintroduced in several areas, sometimes officially and sometimes after escaping from private collections. Not everyone welcomes them: some farmers complain that beaver dams flood valuable fields and block drainage ditches. Conservationists argue that such conflicts can be managed, for example by installing pipes that control the water level of a pond without removing the dam.

For much of legal history, an eyewitness pointing at a defendant in court was regarded as one of the most convincing forms of evidence. Psychological research has seriously undermined this confidence. Memory does not work like a video camera; each time we recall an event, we reconstruct it, and details can be altered by later information. In classic experiments by Elizabeth Loftus, people who watched a film of a car accident gave higher estimates of the cars' speed when asked how fast they were going when they 'smashed' into each other than when the word 'hit' was used. Some even falsely remembered seeing broken glass. The consequences in real life can be tragic. In the United States, analyses of cases in which convicted people were later cleared by DNA evidence have found that mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in around 70 percent of them.

It is hard to imagine today, but between about 11,000 and 5,000 years ago much of the Sahara was covered with grasslands, lakes and rivers. Rock paintings found deep in what is now desert depict giraffes, elephants and people swimming, and archaeologists have discovered fish bones and harpoons far from any modern water source. This 'Green Sahara' period was caused by small changes in the tilt and orbit of the Earth, which strengthened the African monsoon and brought more rain northwards. When these orbital changes reversed, the rains weakened and the region dried out, in some places quite abruptly. As the environment became hostile, people moved towards more reliable sources of water, and some researchers believe that this migration contributed to the rise of settled farming communities along the Nile, and ultimately to the emergence of ancient Egyptian civilisation.

As audiobooks have grown in popularity, a question frequently arises: does listening to a book count as reading it? Some people insist that it is a form of 'cheating', but research suggests the difference may be smaller than assumed. In one study, participants who listened to or read passages from the same popular science book showed very similar patterns of brain activity related to meaning. Comprehension tests have also found little difference between the two formats for straightforward narrative texts. There are, however, some important exceptions. When material is complex or unfamiliar, readers of print have an advantage, largely because they can easily slow down, reread difficult sentences and look back to check details. Listeners, by contrast, tend to be more easily distracted, particularly when they are doing something else, such as driving or cooking. Perhaps the more useful question is not which format is better, but which suits a particular text and purpose.

Ada Lovelace, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, is often described as the first computer programmer, although she lived a century before electronic computers existed. Her mother, determined that Ada should not inherit her father's unpredictable temperament, insisted that she be educated in mathematics and science, unusual subjects for an aristocratic girl in the 1820s. Lovelace became fascinated by the Analytical Engine, a mechanical calculating machine designed, but never completed, by her friend Charles Babbage. In 1843 she translated an Italian article about the machine and added her own notes, which ended up three times longer than the original. They included a step-by-step method for calculating a sequence of numbers, widely regarded as the first published algorithm intended for a machine. More remarkably, she speculated that such machines might one day manipulate symbols of any kind, even composing music, an insight that went far beyond Babbage's own view of the Engine as a mere calculator.

A sinkhole is a hole in the ground that forms when the surface layer collapses into an underground cavity. Most sinkholes occur in areas where the bedrock consists of limestone, gypsum or salt, which can be gradually dissolved by slightly acidic rainwater seeping through cracks. Over thousands of years, this process can hollow out large spaces beneath the surface while the ground above appears perfectly solid. Some sinkholes develop slowly, forming shallow depressions, but others open up suddenly, swallowing roads, cars and even buildings. Human activity can greatly increase the risk. Pumping out too much groundwater removes the water that helps support the roof of a cavity, while leaking pipes and poorly managed drainage can accelerate erosion. In Turkey's Konya Plain, for instance, the number of sinkholes has risen sharply in recent decades, a trend that scientists link to excessive use of groundwater for irrigation during droughts.

Over the past half-century, allergies and asthma have become far more common in wealthy countries. One influential explanation, known as the hygiene hypothesis, was proposed in 1989 by the epidemiologist David Strachan, who noticed that children from larger families were less likely to develop hay fever. He suggested that early exposure to infections from older siblings might train the immune system, and that cleaner modern homes deprived children of this training. Later research supported the general idea but refined it considerably. Children who grow up on traditional farms, surrounded by animals and a rich variety of microbes, have particularly low rates of allergy. However, scientists now emphasise that the key is exposure to harmless environmental microbes, not to dangerous infections, and many prefer the term 'old friends hypothesis'. This distinction matters: it would be a serious mistake to conclude that washing hands or cleaning kitchens is bad for health.

In the 1960s, the biologist Roger Payne listened to recordings made by a US Navy engineer and realised that humpback whales were producing long, complex sequences of sounds that repeated in a structured way. He called them 'songs'. The 1970 album of these recordings became a surprise bestseller and helped to inspire the campaign to stop commercial whaling. Only male humpbacks sing, mostly during the breeding season, which suggests the songs play a role in attracting mates or competing with rivals. What fascinates scientists is that all the males in a population sing roughly the same song, and that the song gradually changes over time. Occasionally, a completely new song spreads from one population to another across an ocean, replacing the old one within a couple of years. Such rapid cultural transmission is rarely seen outside humans.

Gamification, the use of game elements such as points, badges and leaderboards in non-game contexts, has become increasingly common in education. Language learning apps, for example, reward users with streaks for studying every day, and many teachers award digital badges for completed tasks. Advocates argue that these features make learning more engaging and motivate students who might otherwise lose interest. Research does show short-term increases in participation. However, psychologists have long warned that external rewards can sometimes undermine intrinsic motivation, the desire to do something because it is interesting in itself. If students come to see learning mainly as a way to earn points, their interest may fade once the rewards are removed. Leaderboards pose a further risk, as they may discourage those who consistently appear near the bottom. Well-designed gamification, experts suggest, should highlight progress and mastery rather than competition.

The Voynich manuscript, named after the book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, who acquired it in 1912, is often called the world's most mysterious book. Its roughly 240 pages are filled with an unknown script and illustrations of unidentifiable plants, astronomical diagrams and women bathing in green pools. Radiocarbon dating of its parchment in 2009 showed that it was made in the early fifteenth century, which ruled out the theory that Voynich himself had forged it. Countless codebreakers, including specialists who cracked enemy ciphers during the Second World War, have failed to decipher it. Statistical analyses reveal that the text has some features of natural languages, such as word frequencies similar to those found in real texts, yet it also contains odd repetitions rarely seen in any known language. As a result, opinions remain divided between those who believe it hides a real message and those who suspect it is an elaborate hoax.

Almost everyone has experienced it: you see someone yawn, and moments later you find yourself yawning too. Contagious yawning has been observed not only in humans but also in chimpanzees, bonobos and, according to some studies, dogs, which may even catch yawns from their owners. Interestingly, the phenomenon does not appear in children until about the age of four or five, around the time they begin to develop the ability to understand what others are thinking and feeling. Several studies have found that people are more likely to catch a yawn from family members and friends than from strangers. For this reason, many researchers believe that contagious yawning is linked to empathy. However, the link remains debated, as other experiments have found that age and tiredness predict susceptibility better than scores on empathy tests. Why we yawn in the first place is also uncertain; one theory proposes that it helps to cool the brain.

The term 'food desert' refers to an area, usually a low-income urban neighbourhood, where residents have limited access to affordable, nutritious food. Such areas may have plenty of fast-food outlets and convenience stores selling processed snacks, but no supermarket within easy reach offering fresh fruit and vegetables. Because diets high in processed food are linked to obesity and diabetes, food deserts have been blamed for health inequalities between rich and poor districts. In response, several American cities offered incentives to encourage supermarkets to open in these neighbourhoods. The results, however, were disappointing. Studies found that residents' diets hardly changed after a new supermarket arrived. Researchers concluded that access is only part of the problem; income, time, cooking skills and long-established habits also shape what people buy. Some experts therefore suggest that the term 'food desert' can be misleading, since it implies that simply building shops will solve the problem.

Stonehenge, the prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England, was built in several stages over about 1,500 years, beginning around 3000 BC. Its most striking feature is a circle of huge sandstone blocks called sarsens, some weighing around 25 tonnes. Recent chemical analysis has shown that most of these came from woods about 25 kilometres to the north. Even more remarkable are the smaller 'bluestones', which were transported roughly 225 kilometres from the Preseli Hills in Wales, probably using wooden sledges and rollers, although the exact method remains unknown. The monument's main axis is aligned with the sunrise at the summer solstice and the sunset at the winter solstice, which suggests that it had a calendar or ceremonial function. Excavations of nearby settlements have found large quantities of pig bones from animals slaughtered in midwinter, indicating that great feasts were held there at that time of year.

Nuclear fusion, the process that powers the Sun, has long been described as the ultimate source of clean energy. By forcing light atoms of hydrogen to combine into helium, a fusion reactor could release enormous amounts of energy without producing greenhouse gases or long-lived radioactive waste, and its fuel can be extracted from seawater. The challenge is recreating the conditions of a star on Earth: the fuel must be heated to over 100 million degrees Celsius and held in place by powerful magnetic fields or lasers. For decades, experiments consumed more energy than they produced, prompting the old joke that fusion is always thirty years away. In 2022, however, researchers at a laboratory in California announced that, for the first time, a fusion reaction had released more energy than the lasers delivered to the fuel. While this was a genuine milestone, the facility as a whole still used far more electricity than it generated, and commercial power plants remain decades away.

The cheetah is the fastest land animal, capable of reaching speeds of around 100 kilometres per hour in short bursts. Yet its specialisation for speed comes at a cost. Its light frame and small jaws make it vulnerable to larger predators such as lions and hyenas, which frequently steal its prey; in some areas, cheetahs lose around 10 percent of their kills in this way. Cheetah cubs face even greater dangers, and in parts of the Serengeti the majority do not survive to adulthood. The species also has remarkably low genetic diversity, probably because its population passed through a severe 'bottleneck' about 10,000 years ago, when only a few individuals survived. This lack of variation may make cheetahs more susceptible to disease. Today fewer than 7,000 adults remain in the wild, and most of them live outside protected areas, on farmland where they sometimes come into conflict with livestock owners.

In 1929, during the conversion of Istanbul's Topkapı Palace into a museum, researchers found a fragment of a world map painted on gazelle-skin parchment. Drawn in 1513 by the Ottoman admiral and cartographer Piri Reis, it shows parts of the western coasts of Europe and North Africa and the eastern coast of South America with remarkable accuracy for its time. Piri Reis wrote in notes on the map that he had compiled it from about twenty sources, including Ptolemaic maps, Arab and Portuguese charts, and a map drawn by Christopher Columbus. This last claim has attracted particular interest, because no map of the New World by Columbus has survived. Some writers have made sensational claims that the map shows Antarctica without ice and must therefore be based on knowledge from an unknown ancient civilisation, but historians dismiss these theories, pointing out that the southern coastline can be explained by the common practice of bending coastlines to fit the parchment.

Since the 1950s, tropical storms in the Atlantic have been given personal names, and today the World Meteorological Organization maintains rotating lists of names for each ocean basin. The practice is designed to make communication clearer: a short, familiar name is easier to remember and less likely to cause confusion than technical descriptions based on latitude and longitude, especially when several storms occur at the same time. Until 1979, only female names were used, a practice that was eventually criticised as sexist, and male and female names now alternate. When a storm is particularly deadly or destructive, its name is retired, so there will never be another Hurricane Katrina. A controversial 2014 study claimed that hurricanes with female names killed more people because the public took them less seriously, but other researchers challenged its methods, and the finding has not been reliably confirmed.

The influenza pandemic of 1918–1919 infected around a third of the world's population and killed an estimated 50 million people, more than died in the First World War. It is often called the 'Spanish flu', but the name is misleading. The virus did not originate in Spain; rather, Spain was neutral in the war, and its newspapers, free from wartime censorship, reported openly on the disease, creating the impression that it was worst there. Unusually, the pandemic killed many healthy young adults, whereas influenza normally poses the greatest danger to the very young and the elderly. One theory suggests that their strong immune systems overreacted to the virus, causing severe damage to the lungs. Cities that introduced measures such as closing schools, theatres and churches early, and kept them in place for longer, generally had lower death rates, a lesson that shaped public health planning for future pandemics.

Establishing a permanent human settlement on Mars has moved from science fiction to the stated goal of several space agencies and private companies. Advocates argue that becoming a 'multi-planetary species' would protect humanity from catastrophes on Earth, such as asteroid impacts or nuclear war. The obstacles, however, are formidable. Mars has a thin atmosphere composed mostly of carbon dioxide, average temperatures of around minus 60 degrees Celsius and no global magnetic field to shield settlers from cosmic radiation. Its soil contains toxic chemicals called perchlorates, which would have to be removed before crops could be grown. Even the journey, lasting six to nine months, would expose astronauts to radiation and to the harmful effects of weightlessness on bones and muscles. Some scientists add that, whatever disaster struck Earth, our planet would still be far more habitable than Mars, and that the money might be better spent protecting the world we already have.

For thousands of years, people have used homing pigeons to carry messages over long distances. Released hundreds of kilometres from their loft, the birds can find their way back, often at speeds of over 80 kilometres per hour. During the First World War, a pigeon named Cher Ami delivered a message that helped save nearly 200 American soldiers trapped behind enemy lines, despite having been shot through the chest. How pigeons navigate is still not completely understood. Experiments indicate that they use several cues: the position of the Sun, the Earth's magnetic field and, near home, familiar landmarks such as roads and rivers. Some research even suggests that smell plays a role, as pigeons whose sense of smell has been blocked have more difficulty finding their way. Scientists believe that the birds combine these sources of information, relying on different ones depending on conditions, much as a human navigator might use both a compass and a map.

The Library of Alexandria, founded in Egypt in the third century BC under the Ptolemaic dynasty, aimed to collect every book in the known world. According to ancient accounts, ships arriving in the harbour were searched, and any books found on board were copied; the library kept the originals and returned the copies to their owners. Scholars working there made important advances: Eratosthenes calculated the circumference of the Earth with impressive accuracy, and others produced standard editions of Homer's poems. Popular culture often imagines the library being destroyed in a single dramatic fire, usually blamed on Julius Caesar in 48 BC. Historians, however, believe that its decline was gradual. Reduced funding, political turmoil and the expulsion of scholars weakened it over several centuries, and by the time of its final disappearance, it may already have been a shadow of its former self.

About 10 percent of people are left-handed, a proportion that appears to have remained fairly stable for thousands of years, judging from the tools and cave paintings left by our ancestors. For much of history, however, left-handedness was viewed with suspicion. The word 'sinister', for example, comes from the Latin for 'left', and in many countries left-handed children were forced to write with their right hand until well into the twentieth century. Scientists have found that handedness is influenced by many genes, each with a very small effect, as well as by environmental factors, so it is not simply inherited like eye colour. Why the proportion of left-handers has remained so consistent is an intriguing question. One theory suggests that left-handers enjoy an advantage in fighting and in sports such as tennis and fencing, because opponents are less used to facing them, but that this advantage would disappear if they became too common.

In the early 2000s, researchers identified several regions of the world where people live exceptionally long lives, including Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy and the Nicoya Peninsula in Costa Rica. These areas, which became known as 'blue zones', have unusually high numbers of people who reach the age of 100. Studies of their residents found certain common habits: a diet based largely on plants and beans, regular low-intensity physical activity built into daily life, such as walking and gardening, and strong social and family ties. The concept has become hugely popular and has inspired books, diets and even town planning projects. However, some demographers have raised doubts about the data. They argue that in some regions poor birth records and even pension fraud may have exaggerated the number of very old residents. This does not mean the healthy habits are worthless, but it suggests that the extraordinary claims about these places should be treated with care.

Most people have heard of the placebo effect, in which a patient's condition improves after receiving an inactive treatment simply because they expect it to work. Less well known is its darker twin, the nocebo effect: negative expectations can produce real negative symptoms. In clinical trials, a significant proportion of participants given sugar pills report side effects such as headaches, nausea and fatigue, often the very side effects listed on the consent form for the real drug. In one striking study of statins, drugs that lower cholesterol, patients experienced almost as many symptoms during months when they unknowingly took placebo tablets as during months when they took the real medicine. The findings pose an ethical dilemma for doctors. Patients have a right to be informed about possible side effects, yet the way this information is presented may itself make those side effects more likely. Some researchers suggest emphasising the proportion of patients who experience no problems at all.

At the beginning of the twentieth century, scientists warned that the world was running out of nitrogen fertiliser. Plants need nitrogen to grow, and although the air is almost 80 percent nitrogen, crops cannot use it in that form. Farmers depended on natural sources such as manure and imported deposits of bird droppings from South America, which were being rapidly exhausted. The solution came from the German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch, who developed a process to convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia using high pressure, high temperature and a catalyst. Industrial production began in 1913. Today, the Haber-Bosch process is estimated to support the food supply of around half the world's population. Its legacy is not wholly positive, however: it consumes about 1 to 2 percent of the world's energy, and excess fertiliser washing into rivers and seas creates 'dead zones' where fish cannot survive. Moreover, the same process was used to make explosives during the First World War.

Bioluminescence, the production of light by living organisms, is rare on land, where it is best known from fireflies and a few fungi. In the ocean, however, it is extremely common: scientists estimate that about three-quarters of the animals living in the deep sea can produce light. The light is generated by a chemical reaction in which a molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, usually with the help of an enzyme. Marine creatures use this ability in many ingenious ways. Anglerfish dangle a glowing lure in front of their mouths to attract prey. Some squid produce light on their undersides that matches the faint sunlight from above, making their silhouettes invisible to predators below. Other animals release clouds of glowing liquid to confuse attackers, much as an octopus uses ink. Because most bioluminescent light in the sea is blue, which travels furthest in water, many deep-sea animals cannot even see red light, a fact that some predators exploit by producing red light that their prey cannot detect.

The 'gig economy' refers to a labour market in which people work on short-term tasks or 'gigs', typically found through digital platforms, rather than in permanent jobs. Delivery riders, taxi drivers using ride-hailing apps and freelancers who complete online tasks are all part of it. Supporters emphasise flexibility: workers can choose when and how much to work, which suits students, parents and people who want extra income alongside another job. Companies, meanwhile, benefit from being able to scale their workforce up or down instantly. Critics, however, point out that most platforms classify workers as independent contractors rather than employees. As a result, they are usually not entitled to a minimum wage, sick pay or holiday pay, and they bear costs such as fuel and vehicle maintenance themselves. Courts in several countries, including the United Kingdom, have ruled that some gig workers should be treated as employees, and the debate over their legal status is far from settled.

Çatalhöyük, on the Konya Plain in central Turkey, was one of the world's largest and best-preserved Neolithic settlements. Occupied from about 7100 to 5700 BC, it may have housed between 3,000 and 8,000 people at its peak. Its layout was unusual: the mud-brick houses were packed tightly together without streets between them, and residents entered their homes through openings in the roofs, using ladders. The rooftops probably served as public spaces for walking and working. Inside, many walls were decorated with paintings and plaster reliefs, including images of bulls and hunting scenes, and the dead were often buried beneath the floors of houses. Perhaps most intriguing is the evidence of social equality. Archaeologists have found no palaces, temples or clearly wealthier houses, and analyses of skeletons suggest that men and women had similar diets and did similar kinds of work, pointing to a society without strong divisions of rank or gender.

Grade inflation is the tendency for average grades to rise over time without a corresponding improvement in students' knowledge or skills. In many countries, the proportion of university students receiving top degrees has increased dramatically in recent decades. In the United Kingdom, for example, the share of students awarded first-class degrees more than doubled in the decade after 2010. Universities attribute part of this rise to better teaching and more motivated students, but many observers are unconvinced. They argue that competition for students, who now pay high tuition fees, gives institutions an incentive to award better grades, and that teachers who are evaluated partly through student satisfaction surveys may be reluctant to mark strictly. The consequences are significant. When too many students receive the highest grades, employers find it harder to distinguish between candidates, and genuinely outstanding students lose the recognition they deserve.

Cloud seeding is a technique that aims to increase rainfall or snowfall by releasing tiny particles, usually silver iodide, into clouds from aircraft or ground-based generators. The particles act as nuclei around which water droplets or ice crystals can form, helping them become heavy enough to fall. The method was first demonstrated in the United States in 1946, and today more than fifty countries have used it, including the United Arab Emirates, which runs dozens of missions every year, and China, which has used it to clear skies before major events such as the 2008 Beijing Olympics. Measuring its effectiveness, however, is surprisingly difficult. Since no one can know how much rain a cloud would have produced without intervention, researchers must rely on statistical comparisons, and results have varied. A carefully designed 2017 study in Idaho did provide direct evidence that seeding produced snowfall, but experts caution that it works only when suitable clouds are already present; it cannot create rain from a clear sky.

Lightning strikes the Earth about 40 to 50 times every second, amounting to more than a billion flashes a year. It occurs when collisions between ice particles inside storm clouds separate electric charges, typically leaving the top of the cloud positively charged and the bottom negatively charged. When the difference becomes large enough, the air, normally an insulator, breaks down and a giant spark flashes within the cloud or towards the ground. A single bolt can heat the surrounding air to around 30,000 degrees Celsius, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun, causing it to expand explosively and produce thunder. Contrary to the popular saying, lightning can and often does strike the same place twice; tall structures such as the Empire State Building are hit around twenty times a year. The best advice during a storm is to go indoors or into a hard-topped vehicle, since sheltering under an isolated tree greatly increases the risk of being struck.

In the late 1960s, the psychologist Walter Mischel offered young children at Stanford University's nursery school a simple choice: they could eat one marshmallow immediately, or wait alone for about fifteen minutes and receive two. Follow-up studies years later reported that children who had waited longer tended to have higher exam scores and better health as adults. The 'marshmallow test' became famous as evidence that self-control in early childhood predicts success in life. However, the original sample was small and consisted mostly of children of university staff. When researchers repeated the study in 2018 with a larger and more diverse group of children, the link with later achievement was much weaker, and it almost disappeared once factors such as family income and home environment were taken into account. Other research has shown that children are less willing to wait when they have reason to distrust the adult making the promise, suggesting that the choice may reflect experience as much as character.

In 1962, the American biologist Rachel Carson published Silent Spring, a book that documented the harmful effects of synthetic pesticides, particularly DDT. Carson described how these chemicals, sprayed widely to kill insects, accumulated in the food chain, reaching high concentrations in birds of prey such as eagles and falcons. DDT caused their eggshells to become so thin that they broke during incubation, leading to dramatic population declines. The title referred to a future in which no birds would sing in spring. The chemical industry attacked Carson fiercely, questioning her scientific credibility and portraying her as hysterical. Nevertheless, the book caught the public's attention and led to a presidential investigation that largely supported her findings. DDT was banned for agricultural use in the United States in 1972, and populations of bald eagles and peregrine falcons gradually recovered. Silent Spring is widely credited with helping to launch the modern environmental movement.

Facial recognition technology, which identifies people by analysing the features of their faces, has spread rapidly from unlocking smartphones to monitoring public spaces. Police forces argue that it helps them find suspects and missing persons quickly, and some airports use it to speed up boarding. Yet its growth has alarmed civil liberties groups. One concern is accuracy. Several studies have found that some systems misidentify people with darker skin and women far more often than white men, largely because the images used to train them were not diverse enough. In the United States, several people have been wrongly arrested after being misidentified by such software. A broader worry is privacy: if cameras can recognise anyone in a crowd, people may be discouraged from attending protests or visiting certain places. In response, some cities, including San Francisco, have banned police use of the technology, while the European Union has introduced strict limits on its use in public spaces.

Easter Island, or Rapa Nui, a remote island in the Pacific Ocean, is famous for its nearly 1,000 giant stone statues, called moai. For decades, the island was presented as a warning about environmental self-destruction. According to this popular account, the islanders cut down all the trees to transport the statues, causing soil erosion, famine, warfare and a population collapse long before Europeans arrived in 1722. Recent research, however, has challenged this story. Radiocarbon dating suggests that the island was settled later than once thought, around 1200 AD, and that the population remained relatively stable until European contact. Rats that arrived with the first settlers probably contributed to deforestation by eating palm seeds. The real catastrophe seems to have come later, when European diseases and the slave trade of the 1860s reduced the population to just over 100 people. Experiments have also shown that the moai could have been 'walked' upright using ropes, without the need for large amounts of timber.

Fermentation is one of the oldest methods of preserving food. When microorganisms such as bacteria and yeasts break down sugars, they produce acids, alcohol or gases that prevent the growth of harmful microbes, allowing food to be stored for longer. Yoghurt, cheese, sauerkraut, kimchi, soy sauce and bread all rely on fermentation, and turşu, the pickled vegetables popular in Turkey, is another familiar example. In recent years, fermented foods have gained attention for their possible health benefits. Many contain live bacteria that may support a healthy gut microbiome, and a 2021 study found that people who ate fermented foods daily for ten weeks showed greater diversity of gut microbes and lower levels of inflammation. Nevertheless, scientists caution against exaggerated claims. Not all fermented products contain live organisms, since processes such as baking, pasteurisation and canning kill them, and the long-term effects on health are still being investigated.

Almost everyone procrastinates occasionally, but for some people putting off important tasks becomes a chronic problem that harms their studies, careers and health. It is often assumed that procrastinators are simply lazy or poor at managing their time. Psychologists increasingly argue, however, that procrastination is primarily a problem of managing emotions. When a task makes us feel anxious, bored or insecure, avoiding it brings immediate relief, even though the task, and the stress associated with it, will still be waiting later. This short-term mood repair explains why people often turn to something pleasant, such as watching videos, rather than simply resting. Interestingly, research has found that students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam were less likely to procrastinate before the next, apparently because self-forgiveness reduced the negative feelings linked to studying. Such findings suggest that harsh self-criticism, far from motivating people, may make the problem worse.

In the hot summer of 1858, the River Thames in London smelled so terrible that the period became known as the 'Great Stink'. For centuries, the city's waste had flowed into the river, which was also a major source of drinking water. At the time, most doctors believed that diseases such as cholera were spread by 'miasma', or bad air. Ironically, it was this mistaken belief that finally prompted action: members of Parliament, whose building stood beside the river, feared that the foul smell itself was deadly. Within weeks they approved funding for a vast new sewer system designed by the engineer Joseph Bazalgette. Completed over the following two decades, it carried waste far downstream, away from the city centre. Bazalgette deliberately made the pipes much wider than necessary, anticipating future growth, a decision that allowed the system to serve London for more than 150 years. The sewers also ended the city's cholera epidemics, although the true cause of the disease, contaminated water, was only gradually accepted.

Reducing class sizes is one of the most popular education policies among parents and teachers, and it seems intuitively obvious that pupils will learn more when teachers have fewer children to attend to. The best-known evidence comes from the Tennessee STAR project in the 1980s, in which thousands of young pupils were randomly assigned to small classes of around 15 or regular classes of around 22. Those in small classes performed better, with the largest gains among disadvantaged children, and some benefits persisted for years. However, other studies have produced more modest results, and economists point out that reducing class sizes is extremely expensive, since it requires hiring many more teachers and building more classrooms. When California rapidly cut class sizes in the 1990s, many schools had to employ inexperienced and unqualified teachers, which may have cancelled out the benefits. Some researchers therefore argue that the same money might achieve more if spent on improving the quality of teaching.

The kakapo, a large, flightless parrot found only in New Zealand, is one of the strangest and most endangered birds on Earth. It is nocturnal, can live for up to 90 years and is the heaviest parrot in the world. Having evolved on islands without land mammals, it developed an unusual defence against predators: when threatened, it freezes and relies on its green feathers for camouflage. This worked well against birds of prey that hunt by sight, but proved disastrous when humans introduced cats, rats and stoats, which hunt by smell. By 1995, only 51 kakapo remained. A remarkable recovery programme moved all the surviving birds to predator-free islands, where each individual is monitored and named. Because kakapo breed only in years when certain trees produce abundant fruit, conservationists even provide supplementary food to encourage breeding. Thanks to these efforts, the population has risen to more than 200.

Ibn al-Haytham, known in Europe as Alhazen, was born in Basra around 965 AD and became one of the most important scientists of the medieval world. According to a well-known story, he was summoned to Cairo by the caliph to regulate the flooding of the Nile but soon realised that the task was impossible. Fearing the caliph's anger, he supposedly pretended to be mad and was confined to his house for about ten years, during which he wrote much of his great work, the Book of Optics. In it, he rejected the ancient Greek theory that the eye sends out rays to see objects, arguing instead that vision occurs when light reflected from objects enters the eye. More importantly, he insisted that theories should be tested through systematic, repeatable experiments, which is why many historians regard him as a pioneer of the scientific method. Translated into Latin, his work influenced European thinkers such as Roger Bacon and Johannes Kepler.

Salt is essential for life; the body needs sodium to regulate fluids and to allow nerves and muscles to function. Yet most people today consume far more than they need. The World Health Organization recommends less than 5 grams of salt a day, about one teaspoon, but average intake in many countries is roughly double that. Excess sodium raises blood pressure, a major risk factor for heart attacks and strokes. What many consumers do not realise is that most of the salt they eat does not come from the salt shaker. In industrialised countries, around three-quarters is already present in processed foods such as bread, cheese, sauces and ready meals, often in products that do not taste particularly salty. For this reason, several governments have negotiated with food manufacturers to reduce salt gradually. The United Kingdom's programme, which lowered salt levels in many products step by step so that consumers hardly noticed, is often cited as a success.

People who travel to high mountains often suffer from altitude sickness, with symptoms such as headaches, nausea and breathlessness, because the air contains less oxygen. Populations that have lived at high altitude for thousands of years, however, have adapted to these conditions, and remarkably, they have done so in different ways. Andean highlanders in South America tend to have higher concentrations of haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in the blood. Tibetans, by contrast, generally do not have high haemoglobin levels; instead, they breathe more rapidly and have wider blood vessels that increase blood flow. Researchers discovered that many Tibetans carry a version of a gene called EPAS1 that appears to have been inherited from the Denisovans, an extinct group of ancient humans. Having high haemoglobin is not always an advantage, since it thickens the blood and can increase the risk of heart problems, which may explain why the Tibetan solution seems to cause fewer health complications.

Museums in Europe and North America hold millions of objects acquired during the colonial era, and demands for their return have grown louder in recent years. The Benin Bronzes, thousands of sculptures and plaques looted by British soldiers from the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, in 1897, have become a symbol of the debate. Supporters of restitution argue that such objects were taken by force and that they hold deep cultural and spiritual significance for the communities they came from. Some museums have resisted, arguing that they preserve these treasures for all humanity and make them accessible to millions of visitors. They have also questioned whether the objects would be properly protected if returned. Such arguments, however, are losing ground. In 2022, Germany transferred ownership of more than 1,000 Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, and several other institutions have followed. The question increasingly seems to be not whether objects should be returned, but how and when.

El Niño is a climate pattern that occurs every two to seven years when surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become unusually warm. The name, meaning 'the boy' in Spanish, was given by Peruvian fishermen who noticed that the warm water often appeared around Christmas. Normally, trade winds push warm surface water westwards towards Asia, allowing cold, nutrient-rich water to rise along the coast of South America. During El Niño, these winds weaken, and the warm water spreads back eastwards. The effects are felt around the world. Peru and Ecuador may experience heavy rain and flooding, while Australia, Indonesia and southern Africa often suffer droughts. The cold, nutrient-rich waters that support huge fish populations off Peru are suppressed, which can devastate the fishing industry. Since the warm ocean releases heat into the atmosphere, global temperatures also tend to rise during strong El Niño years.

In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick announced that DNA has the structure of a double helix, a discovery that transformed biology and earned them, together with Maurice Wilkins, the Nobel Prize in 1962. Largely missing from the celebrations was Rosalind Franklin, a British chemist whose X-ray images of DNA had been crucial to the breakthrough. Her most famous image, known as Photo 51, clearly indicated a helical structure. Without her knowledge, Wilkins, a colleague with whom she had a difficult relationship, showed the image to Watson, and data from her unpublished report also reached Watson and Crick. Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at the age of 37, possibly as a result of her exposure to radiation, and Nobel Prizes are not awarded after death. For decades her role was underestimated, partly because of Watson's dismissive portrayal of her in his memoir. Today she is widely recognised as a key contributor to one of science's greatest discoveries.

Many businesses choose colours carefully, believing that they influence how customers feel and behave. Fast-food chains often use red and yellow, supposedly because these colours stimulate appetite and a sense of urgency, while banks favour blue to suggest trust and stability. Some findings support the idea that colour matters. In several experiments, people rated identical products differently depending on the colour of the packaging, and sports teams wearing red have been reported to win slightly more often in certain competitions. However, much popular advice about colour psychology rests on weak evidence. Many studies have used small samples, and their results have often failed to replicate. Moreover, the meanings of colours vary between cultures: white is associated with weddings in many Western countries but with mourning in parts of East Asia. Researchers generally agree that context is crucial; the same colour can produce very different reactions depending on the product, the setting and the viewer's background.

As roads, farms and cities expand, natural habitats are increasingly broken into small, isolated patches. This fragmentation is a serious threat to wildlife, because animals trapped in small areas may be unable to find enough food, mates or new territory, and isolated populations can suffer from inbreeding. One solution is to create wildlife corridors, strips of habitat that link separate areas and allow animals to move between them. These range from hedgerows connecting woodlands to large bridges built over motorways. In Banff National Park in Canada, more than forty overpasses and underpasses have been built across a busy highway. Monitoring has shown that bears, wolves, deer and many other species use them regularly, and collisions between vehicles and large animals have fallen by more than 80 percent. Corridors are not a cure-all, since some species avoid them and poorly designed ones can channel animals towards predators, but they have become a central tool of modern conservation.

During the twentieth century, average scores on IQ tests rose steadily in many countries, by about three points per decade. This trend is known as the Flynn effect, after the political scientist James Flynn, who documented it in the 1980s. Since genes cannot change so quickly, the rise must have environmental causes. Suggested explanations include better nutrition, more years of schooling, smaller families and an increasingly complex environment that trains people in abstract thinking. Flynn himself argued that people did not become more intelligent in any simple sense; rather, modern life encouraged the kinds of reasoning that IQ tests measure, such as classifying objects into abstract categories. Intriguingly, since the 1990s several countries, including Norway and Denmark, have recorded a reversal, with scores falling slightly among younger generations. Studies comparing brothers suggest that this decline, too, is caused by environmental rather than genetic factors, although researchers disagree about which ones.
